summary: This is a domain class: a blueprint that describes one song by bundling its title, artist, genre, and energy level into a single object. Classes like this give a program a vocabulary of its own, so a playlist can be a list of Songs rather than a tangle of loose strings and numbers.

lines.text: Each song carries its own copy of this field. Marking it `private` means only code inside `Song` can touch it directly, so a song's title can never be corrupted from the outside.
Energy is a number rather than text because you will want to compare and sort by it later, and numbers compare naturally.

lines.text: The constructor is the only way to build a `Song`, and it demands all four values up front. That guarantees there is no such thing as a half-filled song object.
The parameter and the field share the name `title`, so `this.title` says "the field belonging to this object" while the bare `title` means the value just passed in.
A getter hands out the stored value without letting callers replace it. Written on one line because the body is a single trivial statement.
This annotation tells the compiler you intend to replace a method inherited from `Object`. If you misspell the method name, the build fails instead of silently creating a new unused method.

Every Java object inherits a `toString`, and by default it prints something useless like `Song@1b6d3586`. Overriding it means printing a song, or a whole list of songs, produces something a human can read.
String concatenation with `+` stitches the fields into one readable line; the expression continues on the next line, which Java allows because the statement is not finished until the semicolon.
